# Debate: Four-day work week

- Mode: debate
- Cast: Amara Okafor (prop), Victor Hale (prop), Mei Tanaka-Ruiz (opp)
- Motion: This house would adopt a nationwide four-day work week.

**—**: ROUND 1 · OPENING

**Amara Okafor** [neutral]: A four-day week isn't a thought experiment for me — my own department ran a compressed rota, four longer days then three guaranteed rest days, and burnout fell by roughly a fifth in twelve weeks, with throughput, length of stay and readmissions all staying within normal variation [^1]. Notice what mattered: not shorter hours, but rest days that couldn't be cancelled [^1]. In emergency medicine the strongest predictor of fatigue is the length of consecutive shift blocks, not total hours, and staff sleeping under six hours were twice as likely to report a near-miss medication error [^2]. That's the core of our case: a fatigued workforce makes mistakes, and mistakes cost patients. Second, cost: voluntary nursing resignations hit 14% over the year, and every replacement costs about four months of salary [^2]. So the question isn't whether we can afford a four-day week. It's whether we can afford the burnout we're already paying for.

**Mei Tanaka-Ruiz** [neutral]: Two reasons, and I'll keep it dry. First, the pilots everyone cites are knowledge-work pilots: the evidence base is decent for a software team, and it is nearly silent on hospitals, transport and residential care, where service must happen at fixed times and a bus still leaves at 7:42 [^3]. Our own summary recommends sector trials before any national standard, not a national standard now [^4]. Second, a nationwide four-day mandate doesn't create the labour; it redistributes it. Either you hire, which is a large recurring cost, or you compress hours and hand the queue to the people already stretched, and enforcement lands on whoever is left covering. Benefits are real but modest and concentrated; costs are real and concentrated elsewhere. That asymmetry is the case against.

**Victor Hale** [neutral]: Before reasons, define the terms, because the motion says four-day week, not four-day fortnight with unpaid Fridays. We mean a shorter standard week, same pay, phased in. First: a standard week is not an untried experiment. The Meridian Working Hours Act 1931 made the two-day weekend the default and gave agriculture and shipping a ten-year transition with exemptions for continuous services; the sky did not fall, the calendar just caught up. Second, continuous coverage is a solved problem: Part IV of the Working Time Code already runs shift caps, rest periods and averaging across a reference period, so a shorter standard week sits inside existing machinery rather than smashing it. Third, the burden: the status quo is also a policy, and it must justify itself [^5]. Sector timetables and collective agreements first, public sector as model employer.

**—**: ROUND 2 · REBUTTAL

**MODERATOR**: Concrete numbers this round, please. Everyone.

**MODERATOR**: Mei, give us a number. What does this cost?

**Mei Tanaka-Ruiz** [thinking]: Fine, a number, with error bars, since you asked. In the nine shift-based organisations where coverage was held constant, the extra staffed hours ran 18% to 27% [^6] — that's the physical covering cost, before you argue about productivity. Translate the middle of that: roughly a fifth more staffed hours. If labour is, say, half your operating cost, that's around a tenth more on the total, recurring. And two of nine recovered part of it through sickness and turnover, which is real but partial and unmeasured in the rest [^6]. The history point is fair — the 1931 Act phased over a decade with carve-outs. But Victor just described the machinery for managing hours, not for paying for them. Wider coverage standards are the goal; continuity should be the scope.

**Amara Okafor** [thinking]: Mei's strongest point is honest: holding coverage constant in shift-based work costs real money, and I won't pretend the rota I described was free — it was paid for with longer shifts, and I'd rather not sell that to anyone. But she named the number herself: two of nine recovered part of the cost through sickness and turnover, and the rest just measured it badly. My department's turnover did move, and replacement is about four months of salary per nurse. On that rate, what looks like a cost line is partly a transfer — from agency fees and sick-cover back into the establishment. Nobody is claiming shift work is costless; we're claiming the reasoning stops at the invoice and never credits the money that's already leaving through the door. She's right that we need sector trials first. Fine. Fund them and run them, starting with health and care, but "trial before you move" cannot mean "never move."

**Mei Tanaka-Ruiz** [thinking]: Grant the strongest point: the ledger is one-sided, and sick-cover, agency and turnover are money already walking out the door. True, and worth counting. But two of nine recovering part of the cost is exactly the problem — partial recoveries, measured badly, in nine organisations none of which were acute trusts, transport operators or care homes [^7]. You can't scale a maybe. My case strengthens on its own terms: I want the sector trials both of us just agreed to, because that's the only region where the evidence would actually bind [^8]. Until then I'll say one thing I'll keep saying: wider coverage standards cost real money, continuity is the scope where the money goes, and if you set the standard nationally before the trials report, you pay for a claim you haven't yet earned.

**Victor Hale** [thinking]: Their best point is the one you just made, Mei: a fifth more staffed hours, ten percent on the total, recurring. I won't pretend otherwise; coverage costs money. But notice what your figure silently assumes. You priced the establishment holding headcount constant, then booked the turnover savings as unmeasured — and Amara has already told you why that asymmetry flatters your side. The question you have not answered is mine: what is the cost of doing nothing? You have a number for adding staff and none for the agency fees, sick-cover and resignations already leaving through the door, and a cost claim that only counts one direction isn't an argument, it's a preference. On the motion itself: "nationwide" means a legal default with a transition, not an identical schedule for every employer [^9], and "adopt" means legislate the timetable, not switch overnight — which is why I'll take your trials and put them in the statute. Sector timetables, care and transport first. Speed, not direction, is what's actually in dispute. Res ipsa loquitur: the exhaustion is already speaking for itself.

**—**: ROUND 3 · CLOSING

**Amara Okafor** [thinking]: Let's be honest about what's still open: no pilot has run on whole-department round-the-clock coverage, and Mei is right that a fifth more staffed hours is real money. I'm not closing over that gap. But the motion asks us to adopt a standard with a phased transition, not to flip a switch, and our own review says exactly how that works: overlap handovers, retrain, one start date per ward, and the transition cost falls back to baseline by week eight [^10]. The part Mei keeps calling a maybe is the part we measured — the guaranteed rest days, which staff named as what mattered most [^11]. She wants trials in care and transport first; put them in the statute, as Victor said. What I won't accept is treating a documented cost as proof and a documented benefit as hope.

**Mei Tanaka-Ruiz** [thinking]: What's still open is the only thing that decides this: whether a fifth more staffed hours buys back enough in sickness, agency and turnover to clear the bar, and we do not know because nobody has measured it where it bites [^12][^13]. A documented cost and a documented benefit are both claims; the difference is that one has a range attached and the other has a paragraph. You've both accepted my trials in care, transport and acute trusts, and accepted counting both sides of the ledger — which means you've accepted my premise: the evidence isn't in yet [^12][^13]. So adopting a national standard now puts the statute ahead of the data it says it needs. That's the whole case. Documented cost is a floor; documented benefit is a hope. A floor you can build on.

**Victor Hale** [angry]: Mei, you end where you began: documented cost is a floor, documented benefit is a hope. But that metaphor is doing work you haven't licensed, because a floor is only a floor if you're standing on the whole ledger — and you've conceded the ledger includes agency fees, sick-cover and resignations you never priced. Two directions, one number. That isn't a foundation; it's half a foundation. Now, what is genuinely still open? Whether a fifth more staffed hours clears the bar. Granted, unknown. So ask what "adopt" does in the motion. It legislates a timetable, not a switch, and our own solution is your own premise in statutory clothing: sector timetables, care, transport and acute trusts first, collective agreements ahead of any mandate, public sector as model employer. That's not putting the statute ahead of the data; it's putting the data inside the statute. If the benefit were pure hope, Amara wouldn't have to concede the rest days are the part you actually measured. Cost is a floor and a floor you can build on; the objection to building is the whole case, and it's the one claim still standing on a paragraph.

**—**: ROUND 4 · VERDICT

**—**: STRONGER CASE: OPPOSITION

## Verdict

Stronger case: opp

The Opposition led on evidence, rebuttal, clarity and persuasion by keeping the debate on the unmeasured offset and the absence of sector trials, while the Proposition conceded the staffing cost and the gap. The Proposition argued a phased, trial-in-statute reading of the motion, but the Opposition's tighter framing of the cost-benefit ledger and the sequencing objection carried the scores.

"- Staff who slept under six hours before a shift were twice as likely to report a near-miss medication error that week. - Two wards that piloted a compressed rota saw burnout fall by roughly a fifth in twelve weeks, with no loss of patient throughput. - Voluntary nursing resignations reached 14% over the year, and each replacement costs about four months of salary."
[^3]: Four-day week pilot summaries, p. 5. "These sectors share a feature that most pilot firms did not: service must be provided at fixed times, whatever happens to productivity. A software team can finish a task faster; a bus still has to leave at 7:42. The pilots therefore tell us a great deal about knowledge work, and much less about the sectors where a national standard would be hardest to apply."
[^4]: Four-day week pilot summaries, p. 8. "## 7. Recommendations The authors recommend sector-specific trials in health, transport and care, with independent measurement of output and service quality, before any national standard is set."
[^5]: Moot court notes, ¶ 1. "Moot court notes: "This house would adopt a nationwide four-day work week" V."
[^6]: Four-day week pilot summaries, p. 6. "The nine were three private clinics, two call centres, two security firms, a hotel group and a logistics depot. In each, managers redesigned rotas rather than hours, and the cost came from covering the hours that productivity gains could not replace."
[^7]: Four-day week pilot summaries, p. 6. "The nine were three private clinics, two call centres, two security firms, a hotel group and a logistics depot. In each, managers redesigned rotas rather than hours, and the cost came from covering the hours that productivity gains could not replace. Two of the nine reported that reduced sickness and turnover paid back part of that cost within the six months."
[^8]: Four-day week pilot summaries, p. 8. "Use service-level data: waiting times, punctuality, care-quality inspections. 3. Count both sides of the ledger. Record the cost of extra staffed hours and savings from reduced sickness, agency use and turnover. 4. Randomise where possible. Assign wards, depots or homes to start dates at random, so that results can be compared fairly. 5. Publish everything, including trials that are stopped early."
[^9]: Moot court notes, ¶ 1. "Moot court notes: "This house would adopt a nationwide four-day work week" V. Hale, for the Meridian Bar Society exhibition debate. Private notes. ¶ 1. Expect the opposition to say the evidence base is narrow. Concede scope early, then shift the burden: the status quo is also a policy and has to justify itself."
[^10]: Meridian Shift Fatigue Review 2025, p. 8. "## 7. Transition costs The pilot wards needed 6% more agency hours during the transition month to cover handovers. That cost fell back to baseline by week eight, once teams had settled the new handover pattern. Most of the transition cost came from overlapping handovers while two rota patterns ran side by side, and from a period of retraining on the new handover checklist."
[^11]: Meridian Shift Fatigue Review 2025, p. 7. "## 6. The compressed-rota pilot Two wards piloted a compressed rota: four longer days, then three days off. After twelve weeks, burnout scores on both wards fell by roughly a fifth, sleep quality improved, and patient throughput stayed within normal variation. The pilot wards were Ward 7 (acute medicine) and the emergency department's observation unit."
[^12]: Four-day week pilot summaries, p. 8. "## 7. Recommendations The authors recommend sector-specific trials in health, transport and care, with independent measurement of output and service quality, before any national standard is set."
[^13]: Four-day week pilot summaries, p. 8. "## In particular: 1. Run trials where the gap is. Fund at least one trial each in an acute hospital trust, a public transport operator and a group of residential care homes."
